PHY 2049 Laboratory, walkthrough version 2

Lab 8: The Oscilloscope

Send sine and square waves from the function generator into the oscilloscope, then measure each signal’s period, frequency, peak-to-peak voltage and RMS voltage, and compare them with the multimeter and the generator settings.

You will record everything on the answer sheet. Download it before you start, fill it in as you go, then submit it on Canvas.

1Get ready

The goal of this lab is to become comfortable operating an oscilloscope: displaying an AC signal on its screen and using it to measure the signal’s period, frequency and peak-to-peak voltage. Gather the equipment below and keep the answer sheet open beside you.

Equipment for Lab 8
ItemPhotoWhat it does in this lab
RIGOL DS1102E oscilloscopeDisplays the voltage as a function of time and measures it.
Function generatorProduces the AC signal (sine or square wave).
1 coaxial cable with BNC connectors at both endsCarries the signal to the oscilloscope.
1 T-connectorSplits the generator output so it goes to both the oscilloscope and the multimeter.
1 coax-banana connectorConverts the coaxial connection to banana plugs for the multimeter.
1 multimeterMeasures the AC (RMS) voltage independently of the oscilloscope.
1 pair of banana-banana wiresConnect the coax-banana connector to the multimeter.

2Know your instruments

The function generator

The function generator delivers low-voltage AC signals (10 V maximum) with frequencies from 0.2 Hz to 4 MHz. That span is split into seven ranges chosen with the range buttons; the frequency dial then sets the value within the range. For example, with the 1K button selected and the dial at 1.0, the generator produces a 1 kHz signal. The generator can make several waveforms, but this lab uses only two: the sine wave and the square wave.

The output level knob (AMPL) changes the maximum voltage of the output. The output jack is where the BNC connector plugs in to send the signal to the oscilloscope or to a circuit.

The oscilloscope

The oscilloscope is a standard test instrument in electronics laboratories. It lets you observe and analyze voltages that change in time. It has many settings and controls, but this lab needs only a handful of them.

To see the oscilloscope in action before the lab, watch these three short videos (they are also posted as Links 1 to 3 on Canvas):

  • Oscilloscope video 1 on YouTube
  • Oscilloscope video 2 on YouTube
  • Oscilloscope video 3 on YouTube

Coaxial cables and BNC connectors

Coaxial cables are shielded cables designed to carry radio-frequency signals; you may know them from cable TV, internet or audio connections. BNC (Bayonet Neill-Concelman) is the name of the connectors on the ends. Push the connector on and twist it a quarter turn to lock it; this gives a tight connection with low signal loss.

3The quantities you will measure

A sinusoidal AC voltage can be written as

V(t)=Asin⁡(2πft),V(t) = A\sin(2\pi f t),

where AA is the amplitude and ff is the frequency. The diagram shows what each quantity means on the screen.

Frequency from period

f=1Tf = \frac{1}{T}

Amplitude

A=12VppA = \tfrac{1}{2}V_{\text{pp}}

RMS voltage, sine wave

Vrms=A2V_{\text{rms}} = \frac{A}{\sqrt{2}}

RMS voltage, square wave

Vrms=A=12VppV_{\text{rms}} = A = \tfrac{1}{2}V_{\text{pp}}

The answer sheet asks for percent differences using the oscilloscope value as the reference, so the oscilloscope reading goes in the denominator:

%difference=|x−xscope|xscope×100%\%\,\text{difference} = \frac{\left|\,x - x_{\text{scope}}\,\right|}{x_{\text{scope}}}\times 100\%

Here xx is the other value being compared (the generator setting or the multimeter reading) and xscopex_{\text{scope}} is the oscilloscope reading.

Watch your units

The oscilloscope shows the period in microseconds (μs\mu\text{s}) or milliseconds (ms\text{ms}), but the answer sheet asks for seconds, and it asks for frequencies in kHz. Use 1 μs=10−6 s1\ \mu\text{s} = 10^{-6}\ \text{s}, 1 ms=10−3 s1\ \text{ms} = 10^{-3}\ \text{s} and 1 kHz=103 Hz1\ \text{kHz} = 10^{3}\ \text{Hz}.

The multimeter on its AC voltage setting reads the RMS voltage, not the amplitude or the peak-to-peak voltage.

Do the oscilloscope readings look much too large compared with the multimeter?

Run the self-calibration procedure:

  1. Disconnect everything from the oscilloscope.
  2. Press the Utility button.
  3. Scroll down twice by pressing the down arrow (the menu goes from page 1/3 to 2/3 to 3/3).
  4. Select Self-Cal and follow the on-screen instructions.

This can take a few minutes. Reconnect the cable to CH1 and repeat steps 4 to 7 of part B when it finishes.

6Check your thinking

Try each question before opening the explanation.

You set the multimeter to 2.00 V, yet the oscilloscope shows a peak-to-peak voltage close to 6 V. Why?

The multimeter reads the RMS voltage. For a sine wave, the amplitude is 2\sqrt{2} times the RMS value, and the peak-to-peak voltage is twice the amplitude:

A=2(2.00 V)=2.83 V,Vpp=2A=5.66 VA = \sqrt{2}\,(2.00\ \text{V}) = 2.83\ \text{V}, \qquad V_{\text{pp}} = 2A = 5.66\ \text{V}

That is how adjusting the multimeter to 2.00 V gives a signal close to the 6.0 V peak-to-peak target.

Why is the RMS voltage of a square wave equal to its amplitude, while for a sine wave it is smaller?

RMS means the square root of the time average of V2V^2. A square wave sits at +A+A or −A-A the whole time, so V2=A2V^2 = A^2 at every instant and Vrms=AV_{\text{rms}} = A. A sine wave spends part of each cycle near zero; the average of sin2⁡\sin^2 over a cycle is 12\tfrac{1}{2}, so

Vrms=12A2=A2V_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{2}A^2} = \frac{A}{\sqrt{2}}
If the multimeter and oscilloscope disagree by more than a few percent, what could explain it?

Possible reasons include an oscilloscope that needs self-calibration (see Part I, step C), readings taken before the display settled, or the way the multimeter measures AC voltage. Some meters are designed and calibrated for sine waves, so they can read other waveforms, such as a square wave, less accurately. Compare your Part I and Part II percent differences to see whether the waveform shape seems to matter.
